tldr: Peter shows eval-driven development on a JVM agent: golden datasets, deterministic checks, LLM-as-judge and conversation simulations with the Dokimos framework, plus feeding production traces back into failing evals.
summary: Peter argues that agentic systems are uncertain at their core rather than at the edges (prompts, conversation history, RAG chunking, tool and MCP selection, agent-to-agent calls), so pass/fail tests must give way to confidence scores above thresholds. He cites survey figures that 89% of companies observe agents in production but only 52% run evals. The process starts with an explicit goal (what the agent must and must not do), user profiles and happy and rainy-day scenarios, from which an LLM drafts test inputs that you review and later grow into a golden dataset from production data. His demo is a Spring AI Devoxx assistant with venue info, semantic search over the vectorised schedule and personal-track CRUD tools, tested from Kotlin notebooks and unit tests with Dokimos, a JVM eval framework supporting Spring AI, LangChain4j, Koog and Embabel.

His eval pyramid puts cheap deterministic checks (contains, tool-call correctness via Spring's tool-call recorder) at the bottom, LLM-judged ground-truth evals (faithfulness, hallucination, context relevance) and quality evals (tone) above, and humans at the top. A pirate-speech input fails a formality judge at 0.62 until a system-prompt fix lifts it to 0.95; a parking question exposes invented 'ample parking' through claim-by-claim faithfulness checking; a simulated back-end developer filling a schedule passes the judges but fails a deterministic no-overlap check. Judges must be pinned, at least as strong as the agent's model, checked for score variance on a frozen set, and calibrated against human scores. For production he traces everything to Langfuse via OpenTelemetry, collects user feedback, and uses an LLM triage notebook to turn a 'suggested past sessions' complaint into a failing eval. For security he points to red teaming and Promptfoo.
keyPoints: Dokimos is a JVM eval framework with integrations for Spring AI, LangChain4j, Koog and Embabel; evals run as ordinary unit tests with a Kotlin DSL or Java builders.
Build the eval pyramid on deterministic checks (contains, expected tool calls, no overlapping sessions) and add LLM-as-judge for faithfulness, hallucination, context relevance and tone.
Pin judge model versions and temperature, use a judge at least as capable as the agent's model, measure score standard deviation on a frozen set, and calibrate against human ratings.
Conversation simulators with a simulated user, max turns and stop conditions reveal failures that single-turn evals miss.
Production loop: OpenTelemetry traces to Langfuse, user feedback, random sampling, then convert bad traces into failing evals to grow the golden dataset.
takeaways: Write down what your agent must not do, and generate and review test prompts per user profile and scenario.
Start each agent test suite with deterministic checks before adding LLM judges.
Add a feedback button and OpenTelemetry tracing to your agent, and turn every bad-rated trace into a regression eval.
Run Promptfoo or a red-team exercise before putting an agent in production.

quotes.text: We fight probabilistic behavior with probabilistic behavior.
When we create agents, we also get a new role and this new role is agent sitter.

watchIf: You're building an agent on the JVM and need a concrete way to test it before and after it reaches production.
